118.subtitle: Four kinds of knowing, and the mantra named at last

commentary.meaning: This is the verse in which the hymn names its own tradition. Four of the seven names end in vidyā, and they are arranged as a narrowing: knowledge of the self, which any Vedāntin would claim; the great knowledge, which belongs to a smaller field; the auspicious knowledge, which is the proper title of this school and of nothing else; and finally the holy sixteen-syllabled knowledge, which is a particular formula that can be counted. Between the third and the fourth stands Kāma, not as an obstacle or a temptation but as an attendant, and the placement is deliberate, since one of the two great lineages of this tradition descends from him. The last two names then describe the formula itself: it has three peaks, meaning three clusters of syllables, and it is the summit of desire. The verse moves from the widest term available for knowing to a specific arrangement of sounds, and the movement is the argument — that these are not four things but one thing seen at four magnifications.
commentary.history:
Vidyā is from √vid, to know, the root behind veda and, at a great distance, behind English wit and Latin video. In ordinary Sanskrit it means knowledge, a science, a branch of learning. In tantric usage it acquires a narrower technical sense: a vidyā is a mantra of a goddess, as against a mantra proper, which belongs to a god. Four of the names in this verse are therefore doing double duty, and the reader who hears only the general sense of learning will miss half the verse.

Ātmavidyā is the older term. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad stages the classic scene: Nārada comes to Sanatkumāra having mastered the Vedas, grammar, mathematics, astronomy, logic, the science of ghosts and the science of snakes, and confesses that he knows formulas but does not know the self, and that he has heard the knower of the self crosses over sorrow. The Muṇḍaka draws the same line more sharply, dividing all knowledge into a lower kind, which includes the Vedas themselves, and a higher kind by which the imperishable is reached. To open the verse with ātmavidyā is to place this tradition on the far side of that division before saying anything about mantras at all.

Mahāvidyā can be read simply as the great knowledge, and most reciters take it that way. It is also, in the wider Śākta literature, the technical name of a group: the ten Mahāvidyās, a set of goddesses beginning with Kālī and Tārā and including Tripurasundarī, who is Lalitā herself, along with figures as strange as the headless Chinnamastā and the widowed Dhūmāvatī. The lists vary between sources and the group is attested later than some of its members, so it would be wrong to read the name as a straightforward reference to a fixed canon. What can be said is that the word was available in both senses when this hymn was composed, and that both are current among those who recite it.

Śrīvidyā is the name of the school. Śrī covers radiance, prosperity, well-being and the goddess Lakṣmī, and the tradition is named for it because the formula is held to confer all of these along with liberation, which is the claim distinguishing this system from the sixty-four partial tantras. The vidyā in question is the pañcadaśākṣarī, the fifteen-syllabled mantra, and the following names describe it.

Kāmasevitā places the god of desire in the posture of a servant. Two strands of story converge here. Kāma is the archer with the flower bow whom Śiva burnt to ash with the third eye for disturbing his meditation, and in the Lalitā narrative it is from that ash, worked into a figure and given life, that the demon Bhaṇḍāsura arises — so the goddess who eventually destroys Bhaṇḍa is dealing with the consequences of Kāma's incineration. More directly, Kāma under the name Manmatha is one of the twelve traditional propounders of this vidyā, and the lineage descending from him, whose formula begins with the syllable ka, is the kādi school, the dominant one. Kāmasevitā is thus not only a picture but a statement about transmission: the tradition holds that desire itself received this teaching and passed it on.

The fifteen-syllabled mantra is divided into three segments called kūṭas, peaks, of five, six and four syllables. They are named vāgbhava, the origin of speech; kāmarāja, the king of desire; and śakti, power. Each ends with the syllable hrīṃ, which the texts call the hṛllekhā. Trikūṭā, she of three peaks, is the goddess described as this structure, and the three segments are correlated in the commentarial literature with almost every triad the tradition uses — the three powers of will, knowledge and action; waking, dream and deep sleep; the three cities that give Tripurā her name.

Śrīṣoḍaśākṣarīvidyā names the further form in which a sixteenth syllable is added to the fifteen. The additional syllable is treated as reserved for initiation; it is most often reported as śrīṃ, but the sources are not uniform and the tradition has never printed it as freely as it prints the rest. The hymn's own procedure is instructive: it names the mantra without giving it. Kāmakoṭikā closes the verse on a word with two senses. Koṭi means the tip or extreme point of anything, so that the name says she is where desire terminates; koṭi also means ten million, which yields the alternative reading, she of countless Kāmas, and the module records both. The word is also the name of the Kāmakoṭi seat at Kāñcī, a town whose presiding goddess Kāmākṣī has long been identified with Lalitā, and reciters in the south hear the place-name in the name whether or not the composer intended it.
commentary.practice:
Four names in this verse end in the same three syllables, and that is the first practical problem. Vidyā contains the conjunct dyā, a voiced dental d followed immediately by the palatal glide y: the tongue starts at the teeth and moves back, and there must be no vowel between the two. Say it four times in the shape the verse gives it — ātmavidyā, mahāvidyā, śrīvidyā, then the long one — and let the increasing length of the qualifier keep them apart in your memory, since the endings will not.

Śrī is worth a minute on its own, because it is the most frequently mispronounced syllable in the tradition. It is palatal ś, then r, then long ī, all in one syllable. It is not shree with an English r, and it is not the retroflex ṣ. Contrast it directly with the next name, where ṣoḍaśa opens with the retroflex ṣ, the tongue curled back, and then returns to palatal ś two syllables later. Śrīṣoḍaśākṣarīvidyā puts all of that in a row and then adds kṣ: ś-r-ī, ṣ-o, ḍ-a, ś-ā, k-ṣ-a, r-ī, v-i, d-y-ā. Sanskrit has three sibilants and this single name uses two of them four times, alternating. Nothing else in the hymn drills the distinction so efficiently.

Trikūṭā and kāmakoṭikā both turn on the retroflex ṭ, made with the tongue tip curled up against the roof of the mouth, quite unlike the dental t of ātma. The ū of trikūṭā and the o of koṭikā are both long. Kāmakoṭikā has four syllables beginning with k and only the vowels to distinguish them, so keep ā, o, i and ā clearly separated or the word turns to porridge.

Metrically the verse is regular, eight syllables to the quarter, but the distribution of names across it is uneven: four names fill the first line and three the second, with the eight-syllable śrīṣoḍaśākṣarīvidyā taking a whole quarter by itself. The pace necessarily slows in the second line.

In the archanā all seven take the same ending, since every one is an ā-stem: ātmavidyāyai, mahāvidyāyai, śrīvidyāyai, kāmasevitāyai, śrīṣoḍaśākṣarīvidyāyai, trikūṭāyai, kāmakoṭikāyai. After the mixed declensions of the preceding verses this uniformity is a relief, and it makes the verse a good one to use when teaching the dative to someone learning the offering.

What the verse asks is a change in what the reciter takes himself to be doing. Up to this point the hymn has been describing a deity. Here it describes the practice, and it names it as a form of her — so that an initiate reciting śrīvidyā is naming both the goddess and the thing he was given at initiation, and the two names are the same name. For someone reciting without initiation, which is the ordinary case and a perfectly proper one, the verse is still doing something: it is stating plainly that ātmavidyā and śrīvidyā are not two subjects, and that a mantra of sixteen syllables and the knowledge of the self are being claimed as one object under two descriptions. That claim is either the centre of the tradition or its most extravagant assertion, and this is the verse where it is made without hedging.

crossReferences.deva: सोऽहं भगवो मन्त्रविदेवास्मि नात्मवित् । श्रुतं ह्येव मे भगवद्दृशेभ्यस्तरति शोकमात्मविदिति सोऽहं भगवः शोचामि तं मा भगवाञ्छोकस्य पारं तारयत्विति ॥
crossReferences.iast: so 'haṃ bhagavo mantravid evāsmi nātmavit | śrutaṃ hy eva me bhagavaddṛśebhyas tarati śokam ātmavid iti so 'haṃ bhagavaḥ śocāmi taṃ mā bhagavāñ chokasya pāraṃ tārayatv iti ||
crossReferences.translation: So I, sir, am one who knows the formulas, not one who knows the self. I have heard from those like you that the knower of the self crosses over sorrow, and I, sir, am sorrowing. Carry me across to the far shore of sorrow.
crossReferences.relevance: The passage that established ātmavidyā as a term with teeth. Nārada has just recited an inventory of everything he has mastered, from the Vedas to astronomy to the science of snakes, and the point of the scene is that all of it leaves him where he was. Note that the distinction he draws is precisely between knowing mantras and knowing the self — the distinction that the verse of the sahasranāma refuses, by naming her as both.

crossReferences.deva: द्वे विद्ये वेदितव्ये इति ह स्म यद्ब्रह्मविदो वदन्ति परा चैवापरा च ॥
crossReferences.iast: dve vidye veditavye iti ha sma yad brahmavido vadanti parā caivāparā ca ||
crossReferences.translation: Two kinds of knowledge are to be known — so say those who know the formulation of truth — the higher and the lower.
crossReferences.relevance: The text goes on to assign the four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences to the lower knowledge and to define the higher as that by which the imperishable is reached. This is the division that makes the sequence of the present verse legible: the hymn begins with the term for the higher knowledge and then, over three further names, identifies it with a particular formula, which on the Muṇḍaka's own classification would seem to belong to the lower. Whether that is a contradiction or the tradition's central insight is the question the school exists to answer.

crossReferences.deva: शिवः शक्तिः कामः क्षितिरथ रविः शीतकिरणः स्मरो हंसः शक्रस्तदनु च परामारहरयः । अमी हृल्लेखाभिस्तिसृभिरवसानेषु घटिता भजन्ते वर्णास्ते तव जननि नामावयवताम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: śivaḥ śaktiḥ kāmaḥ kṣitir atha raviḥ śītakiraṇaḥ smaro haṃsaḥ śakras tadanu ca parāmāraharayaḥ | amī hṛllekhābhis tisṛbhir avasāneṣu ghaṭitā bhajante varṇās te tava janani nāmāvayavatām ||
crossReferences.translation: Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, Earth; then Sun, the Cool-rayed one, Love, Haṃsa, Indra; and after that Parā, Māra and Hari — these sounds, fitted at their closes with the three heart-strokes, become, o mother, the members of your name.
crossReferences.relevance: The poem's way of giving the fifteen-syllabled mantra without spelling it: each word here is a conventional designation for a letter, and the three hṛllekhās, heart-strokes, are the three occurrences of hrīṃ that end the three segments. Read with trikūṭā, it shows what the three peaks are and why the count comes out at fifteen — and it is a model of the discretion this literature exercises, naming a formula in public while withholding it.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: The book to read for this verse, and the title is a translation of Tripurā. Brooks explains what a vidyā is as against a mantra, sets out the three kūṭas and their names, describes the kādi and hādi lineages and the twelve propounders, and is candid about what the published sources do and do not disclose about the sixteenth syllable.

references.title: Tantric Visions of the Divine Feminine: The Ten Mahāvidyās
references.author: David R. Kinsley (University of California Press, 1997)
references.note: For the second name, if you want to know what the group of ten actually consists of and how unstable the list is. Kinsley takes each goddess in turn, including Tripurasundarī, and is useful precisely because he shows the category being assembled rather than presenting it as ancient and fixed.

references.title: The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation
references.author: Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 1998)
references.note: Read Chāndogya 7 entire — the Nārada and Sanatkumāra dialogue runs for twenty-six short sections and builds by a ladder of terms from name to speech to mind and beyond — and then Muṇḍaka 1.1. Together they supply everything the first name of this verse presupposes.

references.title: Vāc: The Concept of the Word in Selected Hindu Tantras
references.author: André Padoux, tr. Jacques Gontier (SUNY Press, 1990)
references.note: For the question this verse raises and does not answer: how a sequence of syllables can be the same thing as knowledge of the self. Padoux traces the doctrine of levels of speech that makes the identification thinkable, and he is scrupulous about distinguishing what the texts argue from what modern interpreters have wanted them to argue.

references.author: Śṛṅgeri Śāradā Pīṭham
